opus-5.5.text:
That's a good question, and I think my understanding of it has changed quite a bit over the years.

When I first started doing research, uncertainty felt like something to get rid of. You'd look at a problem and think, "I don't know if this will work," and that was uncomfortable. You wanted to reach the point where you had a clear plan and could just execute. I assumed that as I became more experienced, the uncertainty would mostly go away, that I'd develop enough intuition to know in advance which ideas were good.

What actually happened is a little different. As I got more familiar with an area, say machine learning systems, compilers for deep learning, things like XGBoost and TVM, the uncertainty didn't disappear. It moved. The early-stage uncertainty, like "Can I even build this?" or "Do I understand the basics?", does get smaller. You know the tools, you know the common pitfalls, and you can estimate engineering effort much better. But the questions you start asking become harder, and the uncertainty shifts to the level of direction. Is this the right abstraction? Will this problem still matter in three years? Is the field about to change underneath us because of new hardware or a new class of models?

So I now think of uncertainty less as a lack of knowledge and more as a sign that you're working near the frontier. If I'm working on something and I feel completely certain about how it will turn out, that's usually a signal it's more of an engineering exercise than a research question. That's still valuable, but it's different.

The other thing familiarity gives you is a better way to manage uncertainty, not eliminate it. You learn to break a big uncertain bet into smaller pieces you can test quickly. In systems work especially, I like to build something end-to-end early, even if it's rough, because a working prototype turns vague uncertainty into concrete problems. Once you can see where the bottleneck is or where the abstraction breaks, the problem becomes much more tractable.

And honestly, part of it is emotional. Over time you get more comfortable sitting with not knowing. You've seen enough projects go through the phase where nothing seems to work and then something clicks, so you trust the process a bit more. Working with students and collaborators helps too, because you're not carrying all of that uncertainty alone, and different people see different angles on the same problem.

So the short version is: familiarity doesn't make research less uncertain. It makes you better at choosing which uncertainties are worth taking on, and better at navigating them once you do.

r001.rationale: The response says uncertainty does not disappear as familiarity grows: practical uncertainty shrinks, while harder questions about research direction remain.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes uncertainty about execution (whether something can be built and engineering effort) from uncertainty about direction (whether it is the right problem or abstraction).

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, because I think the relationship with uncertainty actually changes as you go deeper. When you first enter an area, the uncertainty feels enormous and kind of undifferentiated. You don't know what's going to work, you don't know which problems matter, and every direction looks equally risky. A lot of that is just not knowing the landscape.

As you become more familiar, the total amount of uncertainty doesn't really shrink. What changes is that it gets structured. You start to understand which parts are genuinely open and which parts are just things you haven't learned yet. And that distinction is really important, because the second kind you can resolve by reading papers or running a few experiments, but the first kind is where the actual research is.

For me, with things like XGBoost or TVM, the useful shift was going from "I don't know if this will work" to "I know roughly where the hard part is, and I don't know if we can get past it." That's a much better place to be. It lets you design experiments that fail fast. You can go straight at the piece you're least sure about instead of spending months on the parts that were always going to be fine.

The other thing I'd say is that familiarity makes you more comfortable sitting with uncertainty rather than trying to eliminate it. Early on you want certainty before you commit. Later you realize that if everything were certain, the problem wouldn't be interesting, and somebody probably would have done it already. So you learn to form a hypothesis, build the smallest thing that can test it, and let the system tell you where you were wrong. Being wrong quickly is honestly most of the work.

There's a danger too, which is that experience can make you overconfident. You've seen a pattern before, so you assume you know how it will play out, and sometimes the field has moved and your intuition is stale. So I try to keep a habit of asking, what would I have to see to change my mind here? If I can't answer that, I'm probably not treating the uncertainty honestly anymore.

r001.rationale: It says that as familiarity grows, “the total amount of uncertainty doesn't really shrink”; instead, uncertainty becomes more structured.

r002.rationale: It mentions uncertainty about which problems matter and uncertainty about getting past a hard part, but does not clearly distinguish choosing what research to pursue from figuring out how to carry it out.

astra-6.text:
I think as you become more familiar with an area, the uncertainty doesn’t necessarily go away. You become better at understanding where it comes from. In the beginning, you might be uncertain simply because you haven’t learned enough. You don’t know whether something is an open problem or whether someone already has a good answer.

As you learn more, you can ask more precise questions. What do we actually know? What are we assuming? Which part would we need to test? That makes uncertainty more useful, because you can start designing experiments around it.

So for me, becoming more experienced isn’t about being confident that an idea will work. It’s about having a better sense of what you could learn by trying it, even if it doesn’t work.

r001.rationale: The response says uncertainty does not necessarily go away as familiarity grows, but becomes easier to understand.

r002.rationale: The response discusses refining questions and designing experiments, but does not distinguish uncertainty about what research to pursue from uncertainty about how to carry it out.

sol-6.1.text:
I think as you become more familiar with an area, the uncertainty doesn’t necessarily disappear. You become better at understanding where it is. In the beginning, you may be uncertain simply because you don’t know what has already been tried or which assumptions matter. As you learn more, you can ask a more precise question: is this something I don’t understand yet, or is it something we actually don’t know?

That distinction is useful because it changes what you do next. Sometimes you need to read more or talk to someone. Sometimes you need to build a small experiment. You don’t have to resolve everything at once; you want to find a next step that teaches you something. For me, becoming more familiar with an area means getting better at choosing those steps, while staying open to the possibility that my intuition is wrong.

r001.rationale: The response says uncertainty does not necessarily disappear as familiarity grows and that one becomes better at locating it, conveying that familiarity does not eliminate uncertainty.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes personal lack of understanding from what is genuinely unknown, but does not distinguish uncertainty about which research to pursue from uncertainty about how to carry it out.
